lessonRef.title: Independent application A: marking the structure of a new poem independently

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops marking the structure of a new poem independently within the unit “Poems, Plays, and Words That Mean More.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's independent application a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
CAST
PAZ, a third grader
WREN, her cousin
MR. HALE, a crossing guard

SETTING: A street corner on a cold morning. A traffic signal blinks. PAZ is searching her coat pockets.

PAZ: It was here. It was in this pocket. Pockets do not have opinions.

WREN: Pockets have holes.

PAZ (checking): This one does not have a hole. (pause) This one has a hole.

WREN: Then it is somewhere between your house and this corner.

PAZ: That is four blocks of somewhere.

MR. HALE (raising his stop sign): Morning. Do not step off the curb yet.

WREN: She lost a mitten.

MR. HALE: Red one? Stripe on the thumb?

PAZ (turning quickly): Yes.

MR. HALE: It is on the fence post outside the bakery. Somebody put it up where it could be seen. (He waves them across.) That is what people do here. If a thing falls, it goes on a post.

PAZ (crossing, half to herself): On a post.

WREN: So the street was helping you the whole time and you did not know.

PAZ: The street did not sew my pocket.

WREN: No. That part is still yours.

(They exit toward the bakery. MR. HALE lowers the sign. Lights fade.)

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Lost Mitten: A Short Scene”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what marking the structure of a new poem independently asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Lost Mitten: A Short Scene,” then answer: Independently annotate the reading for marking the structure of a new poem independently. Which annotation leads to the strongest inference?

Deliverable: Grade 3: an annotated reading plus a supported inference; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If marking the structure of a new poem independently is not yet secure, return to “The Lost Mitten: A Short Scene” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply marking the structure of a new poem independently to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Lost Mitten: A Short Scene.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
